name: Dana Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a cellist. A good chunk of my work is playing as an extra with the Westbrook Sinfonia, which means they book me per rehearsal and concert when they need a fourth or fifth cello. The rest is recording cello parts at home for composers who write music for games and short films, they send me sheet music and a click track, and I send back the takes. I teach four private students too. I love the orchestra days, and I like that the home recording lets me work in my socks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money break down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Roughly forty percent orchestra, forty percent home recording and twenty percent teaching. It's typical pay for a cellist, which isn't a lot. I've got about three months saved, and my partner Sam works as a software tester, so his salary is the steady one. We're trying to save for a deposit on a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop talking about it and get back to practising. I'd probably say it with a bit of relief in the orchestra break room, where it's been the main topic for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my worries were never mostly about AI. The Sinfonia lost part of its council grant last year and booked fewer extras this season, and I felt that straight away. When the orchestra loses its council grant, the extra cellist at the back of the section is the first chair they leave empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Sinfonia's manager directly how many dates they expect next season, rather than guessing. I'd look for one or two more composers to record for, maybe through the online sessions board. I'd keep using the AI email helper now and then for invoices, which saves me an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not dramatic, it's just a hum about money and the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the routine AI stuff touch your recording work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Some composers now use AI to clean up and tune string takes, so they're less fussy about getting a perfect take from me. That's fine, it saves me time. But a couple have said they'll use sampled strings for the smaller projects, which used to be my bread and butter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat deposit if orchestra dates keep shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes longer, that's all. Sam and I said three years, it might be four. We're not in a rush, but his parents keep asking, and that's its own kind of pressure.

say: I'd say we can **stop talking** about AI and get back to practising.
I'd say it with **relief** in the orchestra break room.
think: My worries were never mostly AI, but **grant cuts** at the Sinfonia.
Some composers already use **sampled strings** for smaller projects.
do: Ask the Sinfonia manager for **next season's dates** directly.
Find **one or two** more composers via the online sessions board.
feel: **Uneasy**, a quiet hum about money and the **deposit**.
S0.quote: When the orchestra loses its council grant, the extra cellist at the back of the section is the first chair they leave empty.
fieldNote: Her **per-service** orchestra work already shrinks with public funding cuts.
**Home recording** is slowly losing small projects to samples, even without big AI change.
The **flat deposit** with Sam is the goal behind her money worries.

steps.text: Ask the Sinfonia manager how many dates to expect next season
Find two more game composers on the online sessions board

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mixed picture and we have to adapt, and the government should help people who get hit hardest. I'd be careful online, because I'd rather not look like I'm either cheering or crying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my home recording is in trouble. Game composers are exactly the people who'll use AI strings first, because their budgets are small and their deadlines are mad. And Sam's job is software testing, which is one of the first things AI does well. That's two incomes in one house hit by the same wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI string tools properly, because if composers use them, someone still needs to shape and fix the parts, and I know what a cello should sound like. I'd take more students, maybe eight instead of four. I'd put the deposit savings on hold and keep them as an emergency fund. I'd talk to Sam about him starting a course in something more hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More about Sam than me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam about his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's look at it now, not when the email comes. He'd say testers will still be needed to check the AI. Maybe. My partner Sam tests software for a living, and AI checking software is the first thing anyone mentions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the deposit on hold. Is that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We've been saving for two years. But a deposit is no use if neither of us can get a mortgage because our incomes look shaky. I'd rather have the cash sitting there for a bad year.

say: I'd say it's a **mixed picture** and we must adapt.
I'd say government should help the **hardest hit** without cheering or crying.
think: **Home recording** for game composers is in trouble first.
Sam's **software testing** job is in the same wave, hitting two incomes.
do: Learn the **AI string tools** to shape and fix parts.
Grow teaching from four to **eight students**.
Hold the **deposit savings** as an emergency fund.
S1.quote: My partner Sam tests software for a living, and AI checking software is the first thing anyone mentions.
fieldNote: **Household risk** matters more to her than her own job.
She'd turn her ear into a skill for **fixing AI parts**, a steady person's pragmatic move.
Putting the **flat deposit** on hold signals how seriously she takes it.

steps.text: Learn AI string tools to edit and fix composers' parts
Take on four more private cello students
Turn the flat deposit savings into an emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency support for everyone, and quickly. It's not about musicians, it's about whole households losing two incomes at once. I'd support whatever the government does, if it does anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Home recording and Sam's job both go within two years. The orchestra lasts longer, because playing cello in a hall is hands-on and robots come around 2031, but the Sinfonia's money is already tight. My partner Sam and I would go from two incomes to roughly one and a half, and the half would be a cello.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move us somewhere cheaper, probably back near my parents in Elmfield, where rent is half. I'd play every orchestra date I could get and teach as many students as possible. Sam would retrain fast, maybe as an electrician, because his cousin is one. We'd stop the deposit plan completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A bit numb, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap before robots give you, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of playing in a hall, which is real money, but not enough on its own. I'd be using those years to get Sam trained and us settled somewhere cheaper. After 2031 I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents feel about you moving back near them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be delighted and would try to feed us every night. I'd feel like I'd failed a bit. But Elmfield is only forty minutes from the Sinfonia's hall, so I could still play.

say: I'd call for **emergency support** for households losing two incomes.
I'd back whatever the **government** does, if it acts.
think: **Home recording** and Sam's job both go within two years.
The orchestra lasts until about **2031**, but funding is already tight.
do: Move to **Elmfield** near my parents, where rent is half.
Play every **orchestra date** and teach as many students as possible.
Drop the **deposit plan** while Sam retrains as an electrician.
S2.quote: My partner Sam and I would go from two incomes to roughly one and a half, and the half would be a cello.
fieldNote: She expects the household to lose **a big share** of income within two years.
Moving near **her parents** is the main safety net she reaches for.
The robot gap is seen as **three years** to settle, not a solution.

steps.text: Move with Sam to Elmfield near her parents for cheaper rent
Ask her parents for help settling in Elmfield
Book every Sinfonia date and teach extra cello students
Drop the flat deposit plan for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this sensibly: retraining money, support for people moving jobs, and some support for the arts. I'd say we shouldn't panic, but we shouldn't sleep either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My recording work fades over three or four years, and Sam's testing job probably by 2031. Five years is enough for Sam to train properly and for me to build teaching. The orchestra holds until around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, Sam would start an evening electrician's course, and I'd grow my teaching to eight students. I'd learn the AI string tools to stay useful to composers as long as I can. We'd keep the deposit savings but stop adding to them, and add to the emergency fund instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but we'd have a plan, which takes the edge off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you'd decide the recording work is over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When three composers in a row say they've gone with AI strings. That's my line. Then I'd stop chasing it and put the time into teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger cellist starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to teach as well as play, from day one. Any young cellist starting out now should learn to teach, because a room full of kids needs a person in it.

say: I'd say there's time to act **sensibly** with retraining and arts support.
I'd say don't panic, but **don't sleep** either.
think: **Recording work** fades over three or four years.
Sam's testing job likely goes by **2031**, giving him time to retrain.
do: Sign Sam up for an **evening electrician** course.
Grow teaching to **eight students** and learn AI string tools.
Stop adding to the deposit and build the **emergency fund**.
S3.quote: Any young cellist starting out now should learn to teach, because a room full of kids needs a person in it.
fieldNote: Five years lets the household **plan rather than flee**.
She sets a **clear stopping rule** for recording: three lost composers in a row.

steps.text: Support Sam starting an evening electrician course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and we should use it well. Good training, sensible rules, and support for live culture. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd shift slowly from recording to teaching, and keep the orchestra work. Sam has time to move into something hands-on without a crisis. I'd still expect my recording income to go, and Sam's job too, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as now but grow the teaching a little each year. I'd encourage Sam to start retraining in a couple of years. We'd still buy the flat, maybe in three years, but a smaller one, so the mortgage is easy on one income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can picture a year in 2033 where only one of us has steady work. I'd buy a flat small enough that one cello teacher's income could cover the mortgage in a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools more over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once other cellists do. I'd use them for students' practice tracks and for my invoices. I'm not first, but I'm not last either.

I'd ask for training, **sensible rules** and support for live culture.
think: I'd shift slowly from **recording to teaching** and keep the orchestra.
Sam's job still goes, just **later**, with time to retrain.
do: Encourage Sam to **retrain** in a couple of years.
Buy a **smaller flat** in three years so one income covers it.
S4.quote: I'd buy a flat small enough that one cello teacher's income could cover the mortgage in a bad year.
fieldNote: Even with a decade, she plans around **one income** in a bad year.
Her shift to teaching is **gradual**, matching her steady temperament.
She still expects **both** household jobs to change, which keeps worry alive.

steps.text: Add a few cello students each year
Buy a smaller flat in three years that one income covers
Keep playing as a Westbrook Sinfonia extra

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam's job and my recording work would go at the same time, with no time to retrain. What would help is emergency income support for households and cheap, fast retraining for people like Sam. Two incomes in one flat can feel like safety until you notice both are pointed at the same wave.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about orchestras. Live orchestras run on public money, and if governments get squeezed by all this, the arts get cut first. That's the thing I worry about even in the boring pictures.

headlineQuote: Two incomes in one flat can feel like safety until you notice both are pointed at the same wave.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old cellist** who plays orchestra extras, records for game composers and teaches.
She has about **three months** saved and is saving for a flat with Sam, a **software tester**.
She's pragmatic and steady, using AI **now and then** and willing to learn more once proven.
She worries most about **two incomes** hit by the same wave, from Steady Disruption onward.
Her plans revolve around **teaching**, Sam retraining, and a smaller, safer flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Sam's job and her recording work would go together.
whatWouldHelp: **Emergency income** support for households and fast, cheap **retraining** for Sam.
